meta.title: The Line That Makes Patients
meta.theme: how moving a diagnostic threshold creates patients without anyone becoming iller
meta.learning_objective: recognise an opening sentence by the definite references and the promised pair that every later sentence would otherwise leave unlicensed

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General discussion of diagnostic thresholds and overdiagnosis; no specific text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: An opener item engineered so that each wrong slot is refused by a different feature: an unlicensed definite in the first sentence, a promised pair split from its pair, and an actor who arrives after the paragraph has finished with him.

quality.adversarial_review: The live rival is the late slot, after the two consequences have been set out, where the sentence seems to supply the threshold that the closing sentence speaks of as known. It fails because a committee and its overnight decision arrive when the paragraph has already moved on to what follows from them, and nothing after the slot takes up the actor: the last sentence carries on from the two consequences with 'the same argument'. The slot after the first sentence is the other candidate, since the sentence reads like an explanation of the overnight change; but the first sentence has already said 'the decision', and there is no decision on the page until the missing sentence makes one.

sentences.text: Nobody is made iller by the decision, and yet by the following morning several million people have a condition they did not have the night before.
The new patients are milder, on average, than the old ones, which has two consequences that pull against each other.

Treatment starts to look more effective, because the people now receiving it were at lower risk to begin with; and it also starts to look safer to withhold, because most of them would never have come to harm.

The awkwardness is that the same argument runs in either direction, so no amount of outcome data will settle where the line should sit; somebody has to say how much benefit is worth how much labelling.

missing.text: A committee can enlarge a disease overnight by moving the number at which a measurement becomes a diagnosis.
missing.function: the opening act from which the whole paragraph descends, and the source of the decision sentence 1 refers to as given

question.stem: Where does the following sentence best fit in the paragraph? "A committee can enlarge a disease overnight by moving the number at which a measurement becomes a diagnosis."

explanation.correct_reasoning: Every sentence in the paragraph is already speaking about something the reader is assumed to have been told. The first sentence says 'the decision' and contrasts a morning with the night before, which requires an act performed overnight. The second says 'The new patients', which requires patients to have been newly made. Only the missing sentence performs the act and makes them, and it carries no backward reference of its own — no 'this', no 'therefore', nothing that needs a sentence above it. A sentence that is demanded by what follows and demands nothing behind it is an opening sentence.
explanation.clue_after: Sentence 1 refers to 'the decision' and to a change between one night and the following morning; both are unreadable unless a decision has just been described.

distractors.why_wrong: By this point the paragraph has left the act behind and is working through what follows from it, and the sentence after the slot picks up 'the same argument' from the two consequences, not from any committee. A new actor arrives here and is never used again, while the three sentences above it go on referring to a decision that has still not been made.
distractors.seductive_element: The closing sentence speaks of where 'the line' should sit, so introducing the line just before it feels like good housekeeping.

distractors.why_wrong: Placed after the first sentence, the description of the act arrives one sentence after the paragraph has already called it 'the decision', so the definite phrase is asked to point forwards rather than backwards, and the striking contrast between the night and the morning is left without the event that happened between them.
distractors.seductive_element: The sentence reads as an explanation of the overnight change, and explanations often follow the surprise they explain.

distractors.why_wrong: The sentence sits comfortably beside its neighbours here, but the sentence before it promises 'two consequences that pull against each other' and the sentence after it delivers exactly those two; nothing may stand between a promise of a pair and the pair itself.
distractors.seductive_element: Having just met the new patients, a reader is glad to be told at last where they came from.

explanation.method: For an opening slot, run the test in one direction only. List every definite phrase in the paragraph — 'the decision', 'the new patients', 'the line' — and ask which sentence licenses each. If one candidate licenses them all and itself contains no backward pointer, it opens the paragraph; check also that no promise of a list or a pair is being split by the slot you are considering.

mentor.challenge: The first sentence you are shown already says 'the decision'. Ask who made it, and when the paragraph says it was made.
mentor.takeaway: A sentence that everything refers back to and that refers back to nothing is the sentence the paragraph starts with.
